:::{#thm-quadratic-form-additive}
#### A quadratic form is additive in its matrix

If $\matr{A}$ and $\matr{B}$ are $p \times p$ matrices, $c$ is a number and $\vx$ is a vector of length $p$, then

$$
\ba
\tp{\vx}(\matr{A} + \matr{B})\vx &= \qform{\matr{A}}{\vx} + \qform{\matr{B}}{\vx}, \\
\tp{\vx}(c\,\matr{A})\vx &= c\,\qform{\matr{A}}{\vx}.
\ea
$$

So for a fixed $\vx$, the map $\matr{S} \mapsto \qform{\matr{S}}{\vx}$ is linear in $\matr{S}$.

:::

::: proof

By the distributive law (@thm-matmul-distrib), applied on the left and then on the right,

$$
\ba
\tp{\vx}(\matr{A} + \matr{B})\vx
&= \paren{\tp{\vx}\matr{A} + \tp{\vx}\matr{B}}\vx
&& \text{(distribute } \tp{\vx} \text{ over the sum)}
\\
&= \qform{\matr{A}}{\vx} + \qform{\matr{B}}{\vx}
&& \text{(distribute } \vx \text{ over the sum)}
\ea
$$

For the scalar, a number can be moved out of any product, so $\tp{\vx}(c\,\matr{A})\vx = c\,\qform{\matr{A}}{\vx}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-quadratic-form-additive}
#### Combining two quadratic forms into one

Take $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$, $\matr{B} = \matr{I}$ and $\vx = (1, 2)$.
Then

$$
\ba
\qform{\matr{A}}{\vx} &= 1 + 4 + 12 = 17, \\
\qform{\matr{I}}{\vx} &= 1 + 4 = 5, \\
\tp{\vx}(\matr{A} + \matr{I})\vx
&= \tp{\vx}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\vx \\
&= 2 + 4 + 16 \\
&= 22,
\ea
$$

which equals $17 + 5$.
In particular, $\tp{\vx}(\matr{A} + c\,\matr{I})\vx = \qform{\matr{A}}{\vx} + c\,\norm{\vx}^2$ for every number $c$, because $\qform{\matr{I}}{\vx} = \tp{\vx}\vx = \norm{\vx}^2$.
This is how two quadratic terms in the same vector combine into a single quadratic form.

:::
